title: Frittata di Cipolle
subtitle: Slow-cooked onion frittata
excerpt: Frittata di cipolle is an Italian omelette built on a base of onions cooked low and slow until sweet and golden. The onions are the dominant flavour here, and the time taken to cook them properly makes the difference between a flat omelette and something worth eating.
sourceNotes: The onion frittata is a staple across southern and central Italy. Slowly cooked onions as a pizza or frittata base are a characteristic of both Neapolitan and Puglian home cooking. The dish requires patience rather than technique: the onions need at least 30 minutes of low heat to develop their sweetness.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the onions up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Make the frittata fresh when needed.

content.text: This frittata is built on slow-cooked onions. The onions take 30 to 35 minutes on low heat to go from raw and sharp to golden, sweet, and almost jammy. That base, spread across the pan and covered with beaten eggs, produces a frittata that is much more interesting than the sum of its parts. The active work is minimal; most of the time is just watching the onions cook.

Fry the onion slices in 3 tablespoons of olive oil in a 24 to 26 cm ovenproof frying pan over low to medium-low heat. Cook for 30 to 35 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until very soft, golden, and sweet. Do not rush this on high heat; they need to caramelise slowly.
Beat the eggs with the parmesan, salt, and black pepper. Season the onions with a little salt, then spread them evenly across the pan.
Add the remaining tablespoon of olive oil and pour the egg mixture over the onions. Cook on medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes until the base and sides are set.
Transfer to the grill and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the top is just set. Cool in the pan for 5 minutes before sliding onto a board and cutting into wedges.

The onion frittata is southern Italian home food. It uses the cheapest possible ingredients, needs nothing but patience, and works as a lunch, a starter, or a side. In Naples it is made with torpedo onions, which are sweeter and milder than standard white onions. Regular onions cooked long enough produce a very similar result.
